title: Psalms 9 and 10
summary: The BSB notes that Psalms 9 and 10 together follow an acrostic pattern, each stanza beginning with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet, and that the Septuagint makes them one psalm. Marked here are the verses that begin with the letters in alphabetical order: aleph to kaph in Psalm 9, with no daleth, then lamedh, and koph to taw, in Psalm 10. Where the order would put daleth, and mem to tzade, no verse begins with them. The Jewish Encyclopedia lists the pair as incomplete.

sources.note: BSB footnote: “Psalms 9 and 10 together follow an acrostic pattern, each stanza beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet. In the LXX they form one psalm.”

title: Psalm 25
summary: The BSB notes that each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the Hebrew, no verse begins with waw or koph, verses 18 and 19 both begin with resh, and verse 22, after the taw, begins with pe. Beth comes in verse 2’s second word, after “my God.” The Jewish Encyclopedia records the extra verse at the end and the missing waw line.

letters.note: Verses 18 and 19 both begin with resh (“Consider”), and none with koph.
After the taw, verse 22 begins with pe.

sources.note: BSB footnote: “This psalm is an acrostic poem, each verse beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet.”

title: Psalm 37
summary: The BSB notes that each stanza begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet; the stanzas run from one verse to three. No verse begins with ayin, and the Jewish Encyclopedia suggests the ayin verse may be restored from the long verse 28. In verse 39 the taw follows the conjunction waw, “and.”

title: Psalm 111
summary: The BSB notes that each line begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet: two letters to a verse, and three in verses 9 and 10, after the opening “Hallelujah.” The Jewish Encyclopedia describes it, with Psalm 112, as a half-verse to each letter.

sources.note: BSB footnote: “Or Hallelu YAH, meaning Praise the LORD. This psalm is an acrostic poem, each line beginning with the successive letters of the Hebrew alphabet.”

title: Psalm 119
summary: The BSB notes twenty-two stanzas, one for each letter of the Hebrew alphabet, every verse of a stanza beginning with its letter: eight verses to a letter, 176 in all.

sources.note: BSB footnote: “This psalm is an acrostic poem of twenty-two stanzas, following the letters of the Hebrew alphabet; within a stanza, each verse begins with the same Hebrew letter.”

title: Psalm 145
summary: The BSB notes that each verse begins with the next letter of the Hebrew alphabet. In the Masoretic text no verse begins with nun. The BSB’s verse 13 ends with two lines that its footnote says are supplied by one Masoretic manuscript, the Septuagint, the Syriac and the Dead Sea Scrolls.
